story: October 2026 PCE inflation report (BEA, released Nov 25 2026): headline 3.8%, core 3.3%, vs Fed 2% target

scenes.hook: The Fed's favorite inflation gauge just hit [[3.8%,]] nearly double its target.
scenes.say: The Fed's favorite inflation gauge just hit three point eight percent, nearly double its target. In the next minute, you'll learn what that number measures, and what it means for your money.

scenes.note: Source: BEA, Personal Income and Outlays, Oct 2026
scenes.say: P C E stands for personal consumption expenditures. Every month, the government tracks what households pay for goods and services. Then it measures how much those prices changed from a year earlier. In October, they were up three point eight percent.

scenes.note: Source: BEA · Core = excluding food and energy
scenes.say: Strip out food and energy, which swing a lot, and you get core P C E. That came in at three point three percent. Headline is half a point higher. Core helps the Fed see the underlying trend, and both are above two percent.

scenes.note: Illustrative: a basket rising at the average 3.8% rate. Not your personal inflation.
scenes.say: Here's what that means. A basket of goods that cost one hundred dollars a year ago would now cost about one hundred three dollars eighty. Pay has to grow faster than prices just to buy the same things.

scenes.note: Source: BEA, Federal Reserve. Next Fed meeting: Dec 8-9, 2026.
scenes.say: The Fed aims for two percent a year. Three point eight is one point eight points above that. When inflation stays above target, the Fed can raise interest rates to cool spending. Its next meeting ends on December ninth.

elements.text: A headline number says prices rose. Compare it with the target and with core to see how far it still has to fall.

scenes.say: The takeaway: a headline number only says prices rose. Compare it with the target, and with core, to see the gap. Follow Market Ledger for one explainer a day.
